questions.question: Why does React Native need a separate library like React Navigation instead of a built-in router?
options: React Native apps don't support navigating between screens at all
There's no URL bar or browser history in a mobile app — navigation has to be modeled explicitly as a stack of screens instead
React Navigation is built into React Native core, just under a different import
It's purely a historical choice with no technical reason
questions.explanation: Without a browser, there's no concept of a URL or history stack to piggyback on, so navigation state has to be managed explicitly by a library like React Navigation.

questions.question: How does data get passed from one screen to another in React Navigation?
options: Via the second argument to navigation.navigate(), read on the receiving screen through route.params
Through URL query strings, exactly like the web
Screens cannot receive any data from the screen that navigated to them
questions.explanation: navigation.navigate("Screen", { data }) and route.params on the destination screen is the standard way values flow between screens.

questions.question: In a bottom tab navigator where one tab renders its own stack navigator, what happens when you switch away to a different tab and then back?
options: The tab's stack resets to its first screen every time
The tab's navigation history is preserved — it shows whatever screen was last active in that tab's own stack
The whole app navigation state resets
Nested navigators are not supported by React Navigation
questions.explanation: Each tab maintains its own independent navigation stack; switching tabs doesn't reset or affect the history of the other tabs.

questions.question: What does calling `navigation.navigate("Profile")` from within a stack do?
options: Replaces the current screen entirely with no way to go back
Pushes a new screen onto the stack, with the platform's native back gesture/button available to unwind it
Opens Profile in a new app window
questions.explanation: Stack navigation pushes screens, mirroring how a physical stack works — the most recently pushed screen is on top, and back navigation pops it off.
